title: Example: Influenza in Sweway
text:
The public health institute of Sweway is investigating an outbreak of influenza in the country. This document is a worked example of using the seirvax package to simulate the spread of the disease and to evaluate potential intervention strategies. It follows the course an investigation might take: looking at the early case data, estimating how fast the outbreak is growing, building a transmission model, fitting it to what has been observed, and projecting forward under different measures.
All information in this document is fake and intended for a pandemic preparedness exercise. Sweway is one of four fictional countries bundled with the package, each with five regions and population by five-year age band.
This document works end to end on one outbreak. The scripts in examples/ take the same features one at a time, and are the place to look for the details behind each step:



01_single_population.R
one population, deterministic and stochastic runs, plot styles


02_age_structured.R
age mixing, susceptibility, severity and vaccine effectiveness by age


03_age_and_region.R
combining age and region mixing, seeding, interventions over time


04_scenarios.R
comparing several scenarios with compare_scenarios()


05_fitting.R
the three fitting methods, priors, diagnostics and projections


06_country_data.R
the bundled country data, distances and maps


07_line_list_exercise.R
generating exercise data and fitting R0 back from it



docs/model_description.md has the equations and assumptions, and docs/data.md describes the bundled data.
The exercise uses the following geographical data:


Code
library(seirvax)   # devtools::load_all() instead when working on the package

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(data.table)

plot_region_map()





Figure 1: The regions of Sweway and its neighbours, shaded by population.

title: Example: Influenza in Sweway
text:
Early outbreak
Early in an outbreak the available data is thin. Here it is a line list of about 1,250 individual cases: everyone admitted to hospital (around 200 of them) or who died, plus a tenth of the milder infections that happened to be detected. Each row is one case, with the dates of symptom onset, hospital admission and death where they apply, along with the patient’s age group and region.
The outbreak is generated with a fixed seed, so every figure and number in this document is reproducible; drop seed from the call below for a different one.


Code
ll <- simulate_line_list(t_max = 30, n_seed = 30, R0 = 1.4, seed = 1)
head(ll)


   id date_onset age_group age_mid region vaccinated hospitalised date_hospital
1:  1 2026-01-02     20-24    22.5     S1      FALSE        FALSE          <NA>
2:  2 2026-01-02     60-64    62.5     S1      FALSE        FALSE          <NA>
3:  3 2026-01-03     45-49    47.5     S4      FALSE        FALSE          <NA>
4:  4 2026-01-03     25-29    27.5     S1      FALSE        FALSE          <NA>
5:  5 2026-01-03     45-49    47.5     S4      FALSE        FALSE          <NA>
6:  6 2026-01-04     45-49    47.5     S2      FALSE         TRUE    2026-01-05
    died date_death
1: FALSE       <NA>
2: FALSE       <NA>
3: FALSE       <NA>
4: FALSE       <NA>
5: FALSE       <NA>
6: FALSE       <NA>


Counting cases by onset date gives the epidemic curve so far:


Code
ll %>% group_by(date_onset) %>% summarise(n = n()) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date_onset, y = n)) +
  geom_col()





Figure 2: Detected cases by date of symptom onset.





Growth rate
Before building a transmission model, a simple regression tells us how fast the outbreak is growing. Hospital admissions are the most reliable series in the line list, since every admission is detected, so we fit a Poisson regression of daily admissions against date. The coefficient on date is the exponential growth rate, and log(2) divided by it is the doubling time.


Code
hosp_inc <- as.data.frame(ll %>% filter(hospitalised == TRUE) %>%
                            group_by(date_hospital) %>% summarise(I = n()))

fit <- glm(I ~ date_hospital, data = hosp_inc, family = poisson)
summary(fit)



Call:
glm(formula = I ~ date_hospital, family = poisson, data = hosp_inc)

Coefficients:
                Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)   -2.294e+03  2.248e+02  -10.20   <2e-16 ***
date_hospital  1.121e-01  1.098e-02   10.21   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for poisson family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 147.66  on 26  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance:  20.18  on 25  degrees of freedom
AIC: 118.74

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4


Code
ci <- confint(fit)[2, ]
print(glue::glue("Growth rate estimate: {round(coef(fit)[2], 3)} ",
                 "(95% CI: {round(ci[1], 3)} - {round(ci[2], 3)})"))


Growth rate estimate: 0.112 (95% CI: 0.091 - 0.134)


Code
print(glue::glue("Doubling time estimate: {round(log(2) / coef(fit)[2], 3)} days"))


Doubling time estimate: 6.182 days


Code
preds <- ciTools::add_pi(
  data.frame(date_hospital = hosp_inc$date_hospital[1] + 1:(nrow(hosp_inc) + 3 * 7),
             I = 0),
  fit = fit, level = 0.95, names = c("lwr", "upr"))

ggplot(hosp_inc, aes(x = date_hospital, y = I)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_line(aes(y = predict(fit, type = "response")), color = "red") +
  geom_ribbon(data = preds, aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), alpha = 0.2)





Figure 3: Daily hospital admissions with the fitted exponential growth and a 95% prediction interval extrapolated three weeks ahead.




This extrapolation assumes the growth continues unchanged, which is only reasonable for a short horizon: it has no way to represent the depletion of susceptible people, nor the effect of any measures taken. That is what the transmission model below is for.


Who is affected
The line list also shows which age groups and regions the cases are in. This matters both for targeting measures and, later, for checking whether the model’s assumptions about severity and mixing are plausible.


Code
ll %>% group_by(age_group) %>% summarise(n = n()) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = n)) +
  geom_col()

ll %>% group_by(region) %>% summarise(n = n()) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = region, y = n)) +
  geom_col()





Figure 4: Detected cases by age group and by region.







Figure 5: Detected cases by age group and by region.




Counts on their own are misleading, because the age groups and the regions are of very different sizes: the biggest region here has more than ten times the population of the smallest. Dividing by the population turns them into incidence rates, which is what tells us who is actually at greatest risk and where the pressure per head is worst. We use hospitalisations rather than all detected cases, since every hospitalisation is in the line list while milder cases are only sampled.


Code
pop_age <- population_matrix("Sweway", age_breaks = c(0, 20, 45, 65),
                             by_region = FALSE)[, 1]
pop_region <- colSums(population_matrix("Sweway"))

# the line list reports five-year bands; age_mid is the middle of each one, so
# cases can be grouped into whatever bands we have populations for
age_bands <- c("0-19", "20-44", "45-64", "65+")

hosp_by_age <- ll %>% filter(hospitalised == TRUE) %>%
  mutate(band = cut(age_mid, c(0, 20, 45, 65, Inf), right = FALSE,
                    labels = age_bands)) %>%
  group_by(band) %>% summarise(n = n()) %>%
  mutate(population = pop_age[as.character(band)],
         per_100k = 1e5 * n / population)
hosp_by_age


# A tibble: 4 × 4
  band      n population per_100k
  <fct> <int>      <dbl>    <dbl>
1 0-19      5     720609    0.694
2 20-44    26    1125529    2.31 
3 45-64    68     719078    9.46 
4 65+     106     550951   19.2  


Code
ggplot(hosp_by_age, aes(x = band, y = per_100k)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Hospitalisations per 100,000")

hosp_by_region <- ll %>% filter(hospitalised == TRUE) %>%
  group_by(region) %>% summarise(n = n()) %>%
  mutate(population = pop_region[as.character(region)],
         per_100k = 1e5 * n / population)
hosp_by_region


# A tibble: 5 × 4
  region     n population per_100k
  <fct>  <int>      <dbl>    <dbl>
1 S1        40     181599    22.0 
2 S2        57     581963     9.79
3 S3         7     117303     5.97
4 S4        68    1407806     4.83
5 S5        33     827496     3.99


Code
ggplot(hosp_by_region, aes(x = region, y = per_100k)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Hospitalisations per 100,000")





Figure 6: Hospitalisations per 100,000 people, by age group and by region.







Figure 7: Hospitalisations per 100,000 people, by age group and by region.




The age gradient is steep once expressed per head: the oldest group is hospitalised some twenty-five times as often as the youngest, which is the pattern the model’s p_hosp has to reproduce.
The regional picture changes more than that — it reverses. The region with the most cases is simply the one with the most people, while the highest rate per head is where the outbreak started, which is some way ahead of the rest. Counts tell you where the beds are needed now; rates tell you where the epidemic is in its course.

title: Example: Influenza in Sweway
section: Simulating an influenza outbreak with seirvax
text:
Simulating an influenza outbreak with seirvax
examples/01_single_population.R and examples/02_age_structured.R build up the same model step by step, with more detail on each argument.
A model needs to know how many people there are, how they are grouped, and how they mix. We start by defining the population matrix for Sweway and a social contact matrix. For now we treat the country as a single population, with four age groups.
Population matrix:


Code
N <- population_matrix("Sweway", age_breaks = c(0, 20, 45, 65), by_region = FALSE)
N


       Sweway
0-19   720609
20-44 1125529
45-64  719078
65+    550951


Mixing matrix: the number of contacts per day between age groups. There is no contact survey for Sweway, so we borrow the POLYMOD survey (Mossong et al. 2008) from the United Kingdom, aggregated to the same four age groups.


Code
library(socialmixr)
M <- contact_matrix(polymod, countries = "United Kingdom",
                    age.limits = c(0, 20, 45, 65), symmetric = TRUE)
M$matrix


      contact.age.group
         [0,20)  [20,45)  [45,65)       65+
  [1,] 7.883663 4.047242 1.487512 0.6125562
  [2,] 2.827779 5.667742 2.673422 0.8778406
  [3,] 1.504416 3.869800 3.178423 1.2418862
  [4,] 0.937180 1.922235 1.878675 1.7142857


With the population and mixing matrices in hand we can build a model. Besides those, it needs the natural history of the disease (how long people are latent and infectious), how likely each age group is to be hospitalised, and how many infections to start with.


Code
model <- build_model(N = N, R0 = 1.5, C_age = M$matrix,
                     p_hosp = c(0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1),
                     latent_period = 1, infectious_period = 2, I0 = 20)

res <- run_model(model, "stochastic", t_max = 30, n_sim = 100, seed = 1)
plot(res, var = "H")





Figure 8: Hospital occupancy over 30 days, 100 stochastic simulations.





Fitting R0 to the observed admissions
examples/05_fitting.R covers the fitting machinery in more depth: what each method does, how to change the priors, trace plots and other diagnostics, and what the uncertainty in a projection does and does not include.
Rather than guessing R0, we can estimate it from the observed admissions using the same model. Two methods are shown: optim, which gives a quick point estimate, and pmcmc, which runs a particle filter so that the estimate accounts for the randomness of the epidemic as well as the noise in the data. Particle MCMC is explained, with worked examples in R, in Endo, van Leeuwen and Baguelin, Introduction to particle Markov-chain Monte Carlo for disease dynamics modellers, Epidemics 29 (2019).
Note that we have assumed values for I0 and p_hosp, and that these will obviously affect the fit: a model that assumes a lower probability of hospitalisation needs more infections, and so a higher R0, to produce the same number of admissions.


Code
data <- hosp_inc %>%
  mutate(time = as.numeric(date_hospital - min(date_hospital)) + 1,
         admissions = I) %>%
  select(time, admissions)

observed_age_dist <- ll[hospitalised == TRUE,
                        .N, by = .(band = cut(age_mid, c(0, 20, 45, 65, Inf),
                                              right = FALSE,
                                              labels = c("0-19", "20-44",
                                                         "45-64", "65+")))]
fit1 <- fit_model(model, data, pars = "R0", method = "optim")
fit1


<seirvax_fit> method: optim
  Data: 27 day(s) of admissions, 1 series (all)
  Log posterior at estimate: -63.36
  Estimates (maximum a posteriori, approx. 95% interval):
 parameter estimate lower upper
        R0    1.463 1.425 1.502
  Fitted model: fit$model; see also plot(fit) and project_fit()


Code
fit3 <- fit_model(model, data, pars = "R0", method = "pmcmc",
                  n_steps = 300, n_chains = 1, n_particles = 100, dt = 0.25,
                  n_threads = 4, seed = 1)
fit3


<seirvax_fit> method: pmcmc
  Data: 27 day(s) of admissions, 1 series (all)
  MCMC: 1 chain(s) x 225 step(s) after burn-in; acceptance 0.71
  Particle filter: 100 particles, dt = 0.25
  Estimates (posterior median, 95% credible interval):
 parameter estimate lower upper
        R0    1.441 1.366 1.516
  Fitted model: fit$model; see also plot(fit) and project_fit()


The fitted model can be compared with the data it was fitted to, and with the age distribution of admissions, which the fit never saw:


Code
plot(fit3, seed = 1)





Figure 9: The fitted model against the observed admissions.






Code
plot(fit3, type = "distribution", by = "age", measure = "cum_hosp", seed = 1) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(x = band, y = N, ymin = N, ymax = N),
                data = observed_age_dist, color = "red")





Figure 10: Modelled hospital admissions by age group (points and intervals) against the observed numbers (red).




The match is poor, because of the assumed values for the hospitalisation probabilities and the borrowed age-based mixing matrix. Fitting R0 pins down how fast the epidemic grows, but it cannot correct the age pattern: that comes entirely from p_hosp and the contact matrix. Improving it means revisiting those assumptions rather than the fit.

title: Example: Influenza in Sweway
text:
Scenarios
examples/04_scenarios.R compares a set of scenarios in a few lines, and examples/03_age_and_region.R shows the difference between scaling contacts with beta_schedule and changing the mixing pattern with mixing_schedule.
With a fitted model we can project forward and ask what different measures would do. Projections start where the data ends and carry the fit’s uncertainty: each posterior draw is run separately, and for a pmcmc fit each one continues from the state the particle filter reached, so the projection follows the epidemic that was actually observed.
The baseline is the fitted model with nothing changed:


Code
proj <- project_fit(fit3, t_max = 100, n_draws = 50, seed = 1)
plot(proj, var = "inc_hosp")





Figure 11: Projected daily hospital admissions under the baseline, one line per posterior draw.




The first scenario reduces contacts across the board by 30% from day 40, as a broad distancing measure would:


Code
lockdown <- update_model(fit3$model,
                         beta_schedule = data.frame(time = 40, mult = 0.7))

proj2 <- project_fit(fit3, model = lockdown, t_max = 100, n_draws = 50,
                     seed = 1)
plot(proj2, var = "inc_hosp")

comp <- compare_scenarios(list(baseline = proj, lockdown = proj2))
plot(comp, var = "inc_hosp", style = "spaghetti")





Figure 12: Projection with contacts reduced by 30% from day 40.







Figure 13: Projection with contacts reduced by 30% from day 40.




The second scenario leaves the overall contact rate alone and changes who meets whom: contacts involving the over-65s are halved from day 40, as shielding of the most vulnerable group would. This is a change to the mixing matrix rather than a multiplier on transmission.


Code
protect_elderly_mm <- M$matrix
protect_elderly_mm[, 4] <- protect_elderly_mm[, 4] * 0.5
protect_elderly_mm[4, 1:3] <- protect_elderly_mm[4, 1:3] * 0.5

model_protect_elderly <- update_model(
  fit3$model,
  mixing_schedule = list(list(time = 40, C_age = protect_elderly_mm)))

proj3 <- project_fit(fit3, model = model_protect_elderly, t_max = 100,
                     n_draws = 50, seed = 1)

comp2 <- compare_scenarios(list(baseline = proj, lockdown = proj2,
                                protect_elderly = proj3))
plot(comp2, var = "inc_hosp", style = "spaghetti")





Figure 14: Projection with contacts involving the over-65s halved from day 40, and all three scenarios together.




Finally, the total number of hospital admissions under each scenario, with the uncertainty carried through from the fit:


Code
summary(comp2)[measure == "cum_hosp"]


          scenario  measure      mean    median     lower    upper
1:        baseline cum_hosp 46868.276 46989.966 40230.277 53049.02
2:        lockdown cum_hosp  9103.019  8488.315  4606.415 15129.08
3: protect_elderly cum_hosp 36059.292 36139.923 30226.176 41506.84

title: Example: Influenza in Sweway
text:
Adding regions
examples/03_age_and_region.R sets out the age × region structure, and examples/06_country_data.R covers the bundled population data, the distances between regions and the maps.
So far the whole country has been treated as one well-mixed population. The line list, though, records which region each case is in, and the outbreak clearly did not start everywhere at once. A regional model lets us ask where hospital pressure will fall, and whether restricting travel between regions would help.
The population matrix now keeps the regions instead of pooling them, giving one column per region:


Code
N_reg <- population_matrix("Sweway", age_breaks = c(0, 20, 45, 65))
N_reg


         S1     S2    S3     S4     S5
0-19  38971 134128 27538 309870 210102
20-44 48367 181661 28344 588507 278650
45-64 49018 143773 30591 305795 189901
65+   45243 122401 30830 203634 148843


We also need to say how much people mix between regions. There is no travel survey for Sweway, so we assume that most contacts happen at home and that the rest fall off with distance between the regional centres. Two numbers carry the assumption: the share of contacts made in a person’s own region, and the distance scale over which the remainder spreads.


Code
dist <- region_distances(country = "Sweway")
round(dist)


    S1  S2  S3  S4  S5
S1   0  74 108 158 159
S2  74   0 142  95 122
S3 108 142   0 169 126
S4 158  95 169   0  65
S5 159 122 126  65   0


Code
within <- 0.95        # share of contacts made in the home region
scale_km <- 100       # distance scale for the rest

w <- exp(-dist / scale_km)
diag(w) <- 0
M_region <- (1 - within) * w / rowSums(w)
diag(M_region) <- within
round(M_region, 3)


      S1    S2    S3    S4    S5
S1 0.950 0.019 0.014 0.008 0.008
S2 0.017 0.950 0.009 0.014 0.011
S3 0.016 0.012 0.950 0.009 0.014
S4 0.008 0.015 0.007 0.950 0.020
S5 0.008 0.011 0.011 0.020 0.950



Where the outbreak started
In the national model it was enough to say how many infections to start with. With regions we have to say where they were, and that choice drives the whole regional picture. The line list tells us: the region with the earliest onsets, and the most cases in the first days, is where the outbreak took hold first.


Code
first_cases <- ll[, .(first_onset = min(date_onset),
                      early_cases = sum(date_onset < min(ll$date_onset) + 10),
                      total = .N), by = region][order(first_onset, -early_cases)]
first_cases


   region first_onset early_cases total
1:     S1  2026-01-02          20   201
2:     S4  2026-01-03          18   457
3:     S2  2026-01-04           4   301
4:     S3  2026-01-04           2    50
5:     S5  2026-01-05           9   246


Code
seed_region <- as.character(first_cases$region[1])

# all initial infections in working-age adults in that region, and nowhere else
I0_reg <- matrix(0, nrow(N_reg), ncol(N_reg), dimnames = dimnames(N_reg))
I0_reg["20-44", seed_region] <- 30
I0_reg


      S1 S2 S3 S4 S5
0-19   0  0  0  0  0
20-44 30  0  0  0  0
45-64  0  0  0  0  0
65+    0  0  0  0  0




Fitting the regional model
The model is built exactly as before, with the region mixing matrix and the explicit seeding added. We fit R0 to the same national admissions series, so the regional distribution is something the fit never sees and can be used to check the travel assumption.


Code
model_reg <- build_model(N = N_reg, R0 = 1.5, C_age = M$matrix,
                         M_region = M_region,
                         p_hosp = c(0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1),
                         latent_period = 1, infectious_period = 2, I0 = I0_reg)

fit_reg <- fit_model(model_reg, data, pars = "R0", method = "pmcmc",
                     n_steps = 300, n_chains = 1, n_particles = 100, dt = 0.25,
                     n_threads = 4, seed = 1)
fit_reg


<seirvax_fit> method: pmcmc
  Data: 27 day(s) of admissions, 1 series (all)
  MCMC: 1 chain(s) x 225 step(s) after burn-in; acceptance 0.62
  Particle filter: 100 particles, dt = 0.25
  Estimates (posterior median, 95% credible interval):
 parameter estimate lower upper
        R0     1.41 1.337 1.482
  Fitted model: fit$model; see also plot(fit) and project_fit()




Code
observed_region_dist <- ll[hospitalised == TRUE, .N, by = .(region)]

plot(fit_reg, type = "distribution", by = "region", measure = "cum_hosp") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(x = region, y = N, ymin = N, ymax = N),
                data = observed_region_dist, color = "red")

project_summary(fit_reg, by = "region", t_max = max(data$time),
                measures = "cum_hosp", n_draws = 50, seed = 1)


   region  measure      mean    median     lower     upper share_mean
1:     S1 cum_hosp 63.995069 61.897747 44.138824 85.203650 0.41325192
2:     S2 cum_hosp 28.573332 27.374929 18.123956 40.158511 0.18331257
3:     S3 cum_hosp  5.843311  5.597677  3.703559  8.216688 0.03748555
4:     S4 cum_hosp 35.614027 34.079042 22.379761 50.363885 0.22831320
5:     S5 cum_hosp 21.469952 20.544092 13.489025 30.365699 0.13763676
   share_median share_lower share_upper
1:   0.41405356   0.3975761  0.43354475
2:   0.18311688   0.1779439  0.18738622
3:   0.03744408   0.0363620  0.03834042
4:   0.22796179   0.2197181  0.23500604
5:   0.13742369   0.1324313  0.14169127





Figure 15: Modelled hospital admissions by region over the period covered by the data (points and intervals) against the observed numbers (red).




The model concentrates admissions in the seeded region more than the data does, while the other regions lag behind. That is a statement about the travel assumption rather than about R0: with only 5% of contacts made outside the home region, the epidemic spreads between regions more slowly than it evidently did. Raising within’s complement, or shortening the distance scale, would spread it faster. The regional distribution is for the travel assumption what the age distribution was for the hospitalisation probabilities.


Scenario: restricting travel between regions
The natural question for a regional model is whether cutting travel helps. We reduce cross-regional contacts five-fold from day 40 by swapping in a mixing matrix with a higher share of contacts at home, and for contrast impose the same restriction immediately, at the end of the data.


Code
restricted <- function(within) {
  m <- (1 - within) * w / rowSums(w)
  diag(m) <- within
  m
}

day40 <- update_model(fit_reg$model,
                      mixing_schedule = list(list(time = 40,
                                                  M_region = restricted(0.99))))
immediate <- update_model(fit_reg$model,
                          mixing_schedule = list(list(time = max(data$time),
                                                      M_region = restricted(0.99))))

proj_reg <- project_fit(fit_reg, t_max = 100, n_draws = 50, seed = 1)
proj_day40 <- project_fit(fit_reg, model = day40, t_max = 100, n_draws = 50,
                          seed = 1)
proj_now <- project_fit(fit_reg, model = immediate, t_max = 100, n_draws = 50,
                        seed = 1)

comp_reg <- compare_scenarios(list(baseline = proj_reg,
                                   restrict_day_40 = proj_day40,
                                   restrict_now = proj_now))
plot(comp_reg, var = "inc_hosp")
summary(comp_reg)[measure == "cum_hosp"]


          scenario  measure     mean   median    lower    upper
1:        baseline cum_hosp 45210.97 45121.53 37878.99 50287.34
2: restrict_day_40 cum_hosp 45156.88 45099.96 37614.44 50320.83
3:    restrict_now cum_hosp 44878.49 44791.47 37119.09 50186.25





Figure 16: Daily hospital admissions under the baseline and under reduced travel between all regions, imposed immediately or from day 40.




Neither restriction makes much difference, and that is the point. By the end of the data every region already has its own established epidemic, so almost all transmission is within regions and there is little left for a travel restriction to prevent. Travel measures matter while an outbreak is still confined to where it started, and in this outbreak that window closed in the first three weeks, before our data even ended.


What if one region had been cut off early?
To see what travel restrictions can do, they have to be in place before the region is seeded. That cannot be a projection: projections start from the state at the end of the data, which already has the epidemic everywhere. Instead we re-run the fitted model from day 0 under a different travel assumption, and compare it with the fitted baseline.
We isolate the region furthest from where the outbreak started, cutting its contacts with every other region to a hundredth of normal. Rows of a mixing matrix have to sum to 1, so the matrix is renormalised afterwards.


Code
isolate_region <- function(M, region, factor = 0.01) {
  other <- setdiff(rownames(M), region)
  M[region, other] <- M[region, other] * factor
  M[other, region] <- M[other, region] * factor
  M / rowSums(M)                       # rows must still sum to 1
}

far_region <- names(which.max(dist[seed_region, ]))
far_region


[1] "S5"


Code
isolated <- update_model(
  fit_reg$model,
  mixing_schedule = list(list(time = 0,
                              M_region = isolate_region(M_region, far_region))))

comp_iso <- compare_scenarios(list(baseline = fit_reg$model, isolated = isolated),
                              t_max = 250)
plot(comp_iso, var = "inc_hosp", by = "region")





Figure 17: Daily hospital admissions by region, with and without one region cut off from the start.

The effect falls on that region alone: its epidemic is delayed by weeks and its peak is slightly lower, while the other regions are unchanged. What isolation does not do is reduce the total number of admissions there. Once even a handful of infections get through, a region with R0 above one has its own epidemic, and that epidemic reaches much the same final size whenever it starts. Cutting travel buys time — to prepare hospitals, or to vaccinate — rather than preventing cases, and it only buys time if it is in place before the virus arrives.

title: seirvax
text: An SEIR model with hospitalisation, death and vaccination, built for preparedness exercises. The source is on GitHub.

title: seirvax
text:
The worked example
Influenza in Sweway follows one outbreak from beginning to end: a line list of about 1,250 cases, the growth rate estimated from hospital admissions, a transmission model fitted to those admissions, checks of the age and regional patterns the fit never saw, and projections under distancing, shielding the elderly and restricting travel between regions.
All of its data is fictional, and made for a pandemic preparedness exercise.

title: seirvax
text:
Installing the package
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("Gulfa/modelling_prep_ex")
The package is called seirvax; modelling_prep_ex is the repository. A C++ compiler is needed, since the models are compiled on installation.

title: seirvax
text:
What it does

Age groups and regions, with their contact matrices combined into one structure.
A vaccinated stratum running in parallel with the unvaccinated one, with vaccine effectiveness against infection, transmission, hospitalisation and death that can vary by age.
Hospitalisations, hospital deaths and community deaths.
Contact multipliers and mixing matrices that change over time, for interventions.
A deterministic and a stochastic version of the same model, written in odin2 and run with dust2.
Fitting to daily hospital admissions with a point estimate, MCMC or particle MCMC, using monty.
Bundled data for four fictional countries, and a generator for synthetic line lists to use as exercise data.
